messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Tane, a 48-year-old roofer from a Pacific Island community in California, had been married for twenty-two years. The assault happened three years ago, after a company barbecue. A coworker he trusted walked him to his truck, then forced him into the back seat. The man reeked of cheap beer. Tane still remembers the wet heat of that breath, the steel taste in his throat, and the crack of his own ribs against the door handle as he tried to squirm free. He never reported it. He told himself it was over, that real men moved on.

But the memory never moved on. It stayed more vivid than anything ordinary—the clatter of a passing motorcycle on a quiet street could suddenly throw him back into that back seat, his heart slamming against his chest as if the assault were happening again, right now. Sometimes the emotional flood would hit without any clear image: a wave of terror and humiliation rising in his chest while he was simply standing at a red light, and he would have no idea why. And most unbearable of all, when the memory surfaced, an overwhelming grief would wash over him—not for the event itself, but for the version of himself that had existed before, the one who had trusted easily, who had felt safe in his own skin.

That grief was what drove Tane to start working harder. It felt like the only thing he could control. He began taking double shifts, volunteering for the most demanding roofing jobs, staying on-site until his hands shook and his lower back burned. He told his wife it was for the overtime, but the real reason was simpler: if he was exhausted, he didn't have to feel anything. The busyness became a wall against the intruding images. And when even exhaustion wasn't enough, he started restricting what he ate—skipping breakfast, pushing lunch past two o'clock, eating only a single plate of rice and fish at dinner. The strictness gave him a fragile sense of order, a way of saying *I am in charge of this body now.* He had come to believe that if he let his body feel soft or full or rested, he would become vulnerable again.

The connections tightened into a loop. A news report about a sexual assault trial—trigger. His stomach clenched; the memory surged, grief pressing behind his eyes. To shut it down, he would call his boss and ask for a weekend job, or he would fast the next day, or both. But the very act of restricting eating or pushing his body physically seemed to sharpen the memories. When he was dehydrated and dizzy on a roof, the emotion without image would strike harder—a hot flash of helplessness that made him grip the ladder until his knuckles went white. And the more he avoided through work and control, the more sensitive he became to triggers: a motorcycle backfiring, the yeast-and-hop smell drifting from a bottle on a neighbor's porch. He lived in a state of constant low-grade dread, waiting for the next ambush.

At work, Tane became known as the guy who never took sick days, the one who insisted on the steepest pitches. But his wife noticed he had stopped going to the weekly poker game with their friends, that he flinched when she hugged him from behind. She found him one night sitting on the edge of the bathtub, staring at nothing, a half-eaten piece of toast on the counter. "I think I'm losing it," he said, and that was the first time he had said anything at all. What finally brought him to a clinic was a simple thing: a young roofer on his crew, new and nervous, asked Tane to show him the safe way to anchor a harness. Tane felt a surge of protectiveness so fierce it frightened him, and then a deep sorrow for the young man's naivety. He knew he could no longer pretend the past wasn't tearing him apart from the inside. He was most afraid of what would happen if he stopped running—if the grief he held at bay would drown him. But part of him, a very small part, hoped that someone might show him a way to carry it without having to carry it alone.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not convey that the memory itself causes increased sensitivity to triggers; it shows maladaptive strategies increasing sensitivity, but not a direct causal path from memory to triggers.
